Below are the verse-by-verse notes, each point anchored to its source.

## Joshua 10:1–22 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1
- **Adoni-zedek** means “lord of righteousness” (or “my Lord is righteous”) and is etymologically related to “Melchizedek” (king of righteousness), who reigned at Jerusalem (Salem) in Abraham’s day. The name is ironic: this “lord of righteousness” opposes the true Lord. Precept Austin notes he is an OT picture of the coming Antichrist, leading a confederacy against Joshua as the future Antichrist will lead one against Christ (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-10-commentary).
- Gill notes this is the first occurrence of “Jerusalem” in Scripture. The city was originally Salem (Gen 14:18), later Jebus (Judg 19:10–11). The name Jerusalem may mean “possession of Salem” or “they shall see peace” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-10.html).
- **“Utterly destroyed”** translates the Hebrew *charam*, meaning devoted to destruction or put under the ban. This is a keyword throughout Joshua 10 (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-10-commentary).
- The news that Gibeon had made peace with Israel and was now “within their land” (i.e., living among Israel) especially alarmed Adoni-zedek — a formerly mighty city had switched sides (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).

### v. 2
- Adoni-zedek and his people **“feared greatly”** because Gibeon was a royal-class city, larger than Ai, and its men were mighty warriors. If such a city capitulated, it boded ill for the other Canaanite city-states (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-10-commentary).
- Matthew Henry notes that fear of coming judgment did not make the Canaanites surrender; it made them organize and fight — like a cornered wild animal (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/10.htm).
- Gibeon’s defection removed a key barrier against Israel’s advance and set a dangerous precedent for other cities (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).

### v. 3
- Adoni-zedek sends to **four other kings**: Hoham of Hebron, Piram of Jarmuth, Japhia of Lachish, and Debir of Eglon. These were all important city-states in southern Canaan, each controlling trade routes or strategic locations (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).
- Gill notes geographical details: Hebron was about 22 miles from Jerusalem; Lachish about 20 miles southwest; Eglon about 12 miles south (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-10.html).
- Precept Austin observes that Jerusalem’s leader (called *Urusalem* in the Amarna letters, ca. 1400 BC) wrote at least five letters to Pharaoh regarding his town’s security — political activity consistent with the biblical account (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-10-commentary).

### v. 4
- Adoni-zedek’s message: **“Come up and help me. We will attack Gibeon.”** Gill notes that Adoni-zedek speaks in an authoritative manner as if these kings were somewhat subordinate to him, and he designates Jerusalem (higher in elevation) as the rendezvous point (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-10.html).
- The reason given: Gibeon “has made peace with Joshua and with the children of Israel” — they had gone over to the common enemy. The attack on Gibeon was meant to make an example of them and deter other Canaanite cities from defecting (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).

### v. 5
- All five kings, called **“kings of the Amorites,”** gather their armies and besiege Gibeon. Gill explains that though the inhabitants of these cities included Hittites and Jebusites, “Amorite” served as a general term for the dominant people-group of the hill country (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-10.html).
- Matthew Henry observes that God in His providence gathered these kings together so they could be cut off “at one blow,” like sheaves gathered to the threshing floor (Mic 4:12) (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/10.htm).

### v. 6
- The Gibeonites send an urgent plea to Joshua at Gilgal: **“Do not abandon your servants. Come quickly and save us!”** The Hebrew idiom is literally “do not let your hand drop from us” — a plea based on the covenant Joshua had made with them (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-10-commentary).
- Matthew Henry draws a spiritual application: when our spiritual enemies threaten to swallow us, we are to apply by faith and prayer to Christ, our Joshua, for strength and help (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/10.htm).
- Enduring Word notes the irony: the Gibeonites sought peace with Israel, but it brought war upon them. Similarly, new converts often find that former friends become foes (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).

### v. 7
- Joshua responds with his **whole army, including all the mighty men of valor**, marching up from Gilgal. The distance was about 20–25 miles (32 km) with a 3,300-foot (1,000 m) climb in elevation — eight to ten hours of hard marching (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).
- Matthew Henry notes Joshua’s faithfulness: though the Gibeonites had obtained their covenant by deceit, Joshua understood that his promise obliged him not only not to slay them himself, but also not to stand by and see them slain when it was in his power to prevent it (Prov 24:11–12) (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/10.htm).
- Precept Austin sees in this a strategic opportunity: by defending Gibeon, Joshua could destroy five enemy kings “in one fell swoop” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-10-commentary).

### v. 8
- The LORD speaks directly to Joshua: **“Do not be afraid of them, for I have delivered them into your hand. Not one of them shall stand against you.”** This is both a command (do not fear) and a promise (victory is certain) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).
- Precept Austin stresses the balance of divine sovereignty and human responsibility: God has given them into Israel’s hand, yet Israel must still engage the enemy and fight (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-10-commentary).
- Calvin, cited in search results, would later make the point that Joshua needed this reassurance before the bold prayer of v. 12 — he first consulted God privately; his public command to the sun flowed from confidence in God’s answer (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/joshua-10.html).

### v. 9
- **Joshua marched all night** and caught the enemy by surprise. Gill says he chose the night for secrecy and to reach Gibeon as quickly as possible — about 9–10 miles (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-10.html).
- Enduring Word emphasizes that Joshua did not sit back passively after receiving God’s promise. He exerted himself to the utmost — God’s promises are not meant to replace human diligence but to fuel it (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).

### v. 10
- **The LORD threw them into confusion** (*discomfited*, Hebrew *hamam* — to disturb, trouble, rout). Every verb in this verse is singular in Hebrew, underscoring that it was Yahweh alone who confused, struck, pursued, and struck down the enemy (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).
- The route of the pursuit: from Gibeon up the ascent of **Beth-horon**, then as far as **Azekah** and **Makkedah**. Gill notes that Beth-horon had a notoriously narrow ascent where “if two camels go up… they both fall” (Talmudic reference) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-10.html).

### v. 11
- As the enemy fled down the descent of Beth-horon, **the LORD cast down large hailstones** (*’avnei barad* — stones of hail) that killed more Canaanites than Israel’s swords did (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/10-11.htm — Pulpit Commentary).
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that while this may have been a miraculous hailstorm, enormous hailstones are well-documented in nature. Yet the precise targeting — striking only the Canaanites and not the pursuing Israelites — was unmistakably supernatural (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/10-11.htm).
- Matthew Henry observes the fitting judgment: the Canaanites worshipped the host of heaven (sun, moon, stars), and now heaven itself fought against them. Those who idolize the creation find the creation at war with them (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/10.htm).
- Enduring Word adds that more died by hailstones than by the sword — a conclusive proof to both sides that the victory was God’s, not man’s (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).

### vv. 12–14 (The Sun Stands Still)

**v. 12:**
- **“Then Joshua spoke to the LORD… in the sight of Israel.”** Matthew Henry calls this a prayer of extraordinary faith. Joshua, though exhausted from an all-night march and a day of battle, did not wish for nightfall but for more daylight to complete the victory. He spoke openly, staking everything on God’s answer — if the sun did not stop, he would have been humiliated before all Israel (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/10.htm).
- The Hebrew verb for “stand still” is *damam* — “be silent, be dumb, cease.” Ellicott notes the poetic metaphor: the sun’s “voice” (Ps 19:3–4) was silenced. Translating into physical terms, this means suspending the earth’s rotation while leaving its orbit unaffected (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-10.html).
- Calvin insists Joshua first prayed to God before commanding the sun; the public command flowed from private assurance. He would never have ventured such a bold command without being “thoroughly conscious of his vocation” and having obtained God’s permission (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/joshua-10.html).
- Gill notes the Jewish interpretation that Joshua sang a song or hymn of praise; the Targum renders it “then Joshua praised.” But the plain reading is a prayer (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-10.html).

**v. 13:**
- **The sun stopped in the middle of the sky and delayed going down about a full day.** Gill says if the sun was at its meridian and stayed a “whole day” (24 hours), the total daylight would have been about 36 hours. If it was an artificial day (12 hours of daylight), then a double-length day of about 24 hours. The Apocryphal Sirach 46:4 says, “Was not the sun held back by his hand? And did not one day become as long as two?” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-10.html).
- The reference to **the Book of Jashar** (or “Book of the Upright”): Ellicott explains this was a collection of national poetry/ballads of Israel’s heroic age, also cited in 2 Sam 1:18 (David’s lament). The poetic form of vv. 12b–13a suggests a quotation from that book. Matthew Henry calls it “a collection of state-poems” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-10.html).

**v. 14:**
- **“There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD listened to the voice of a man.”** Gill addresses the objection from Hezekiah’s day (the sun going back ten degrees on the dial): even if those were hours, Hezekiah’s miracle only made a 22-hour day (ten hours backward plus return), not a lengthened day of this magnitude. The uniqueness lies not just in length but in that God hearkened to a man’s voice in this extraordinary way (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/10-14.htm).

---

#### Differing Views on the Sun Standing Still

**1. Traditional Literal View (most Protestant traditions, Catholic):** God supernaturally halted the earth’s rotation (or the sun’s apparent motion), resulting in an extended day. This is held by Matthew Henry, John Gill, John Calvin, Haydock’s Catholic Commentary, and the majority of older commentators. Haydock explicitly defends the literal miracle against those who “devise various means to explain it away” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/joshua-10.html).

**2. Reformed/Covenant (Ligonier):** The Ligonier devotional acknowledges the miracle while noting that the Hebrew verb *damam* (“stand”) can also mean to stop shining — possibly through an eclipse or atmospheric means. It stresses that describing the sun as “standing still” is language of appearance, like our own use of “sunrise” and “sunset,” and does not commit Scripture to a false cosmology (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-sun-stands-still).

**3. Optical/Local Miracle View (some evangelicals):** Dr. Constable’s Notes (DTS) outlines a view that God provided additional light for Israel through unusual atmospheric refraction after sunset, or through a localized light-source like the Shekinah — not a worldwide cosmic interruption. Proponents argue Isaiah 28:21 and Habakkuk 3:11 speak figuratively of God’s extraordinary work at Gibeon without demanding a literal stoppage of heavenly bodies (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-10.html).

**4. Poetic/Literary Interpretation (some modern scholars):** Since the passage quotes the Book of Jashar, a poetic book, the language may be figurative — boldly expressing the truth that God answered Joshua’s prayer and gave him a complete victory. Ellicott notes this view is held by “theologians whose orthodoxy upon plenary inspiration is well known and undoubted,” comparing it to Judges 5:20 (“the stars fought from heaven”) which no one construes literally (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-13.html).

---

### v. 15
- **“Then Joshua returned with all Israel to the camp at Gilgal.”** Ellicott and others note this verse appears to be an anticipatory summary taken from the Book of Jashar. The immediate return after battle was actually to Makkedah (see v. 21), not Gilgal; the final return to Gilgal comes only at v. 43. This verse reads like the poetic conclusion of the Jashar excerpt before the narrative resumes in prose (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-10.html).

### vv. 16–17
- **The five kings had fled and hidden in the cave at Makkedah.** Word reaches Joshua that the kings have been found. Makkedah is in the Shephelah (lowlands) of Judah, about 8 miles from Jerusalem toward the west (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-10.html).
- Enduring Word notes the vivid picture: these five kings who had marched so confidently against Gibeon are now cowering in a cave — a dramatic reversal brought by the LORD (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).

### v. 18
- Joshua orders large stones rolled against the cave mouth and guards posted. He does not let the capture of the kings distract him from the larger task of completing the victory. The kings can be dealt with later; the battle must be finished first (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).

### v. 19
- **“Do not stop there. Pursue your enemies and attack them from behind.”** Joshua urges his men not to let the enemy reach their fortified cities, “for the LORD your God has delivered them into your hand.” Again, divine promise and human effort go together (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-10-commentary).
- This verse echoes the promise of v. 8 and shows Joshua’s military wisdom: cutting off the retreating army before they can regroup behind city walls (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).

### v. 20
- **A terrible slaughter** until the enemy was finished off; only a remnant escaped into fortified cities. The text emphasizes the totality of the rout — Yahweh’s promised victory is fulfilled to the full (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-10-commentary).

### v. 21
- The whole army returns safely to Joshua at Makkedah. **“No one dared to utter a word against the Israelites”** — literally “no one sharpened his tongue.” The Canaanites were utterly cowed. Enduring Word draws an application: the church should be a place where people sense that God will conquer them — that surrender to Him is inevitable (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).

### v. 22
- **“Open the mouth of the cave and bring those five kings out to me.”** With the battle won, Joshua turns to the captured kings. This sets up the dramatic scene of judgment in vv. 23–27 (beyond the scope of this passage), where the captains place their feet on the kings’ necks and Joshua executes them. Matthew Henry sees here a picture of Christ’s ultimate triumph over all his enemies — “those that will not now obey that sweet voice, ‘Come unto me,’ shall then have no other voice to obey but ‘Go, ye cursed’” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).
- Precept Austin notes Joshua made a public example of the kings, exposed their bodies on trees as a sign of humiliation, yet carefully obeyed Deuteronomy 21:23 by taking them down before nightfall (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-10-commentary).

---

## Summary of Denominational Distinctives

- **Reformed (Calvin, Ligonier):** Strong emphasis on God’s sovereign initiative — the LORD, not Israel, won the battle. Calvin stresses that Joshua’s public command to the sun was only possible because he first sought God privately and received divine warrant. Ligonier sees the miracle as genuine but leaves room for non-cosmological explanations (eclipse/refraction) consistent with the Hebrew verb *damam* (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-sun-stands-still; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/joshua-10.html).

- **Baptist (Gill, Matthew Henry — broadly):** Treat the sun-standing-still as a literal astronomical miracle. Gill discusses at length how to reconcile it with the Copernican system, mentions Chinese records of a long day in the reign of Emperor Yao, and refutes the fraudulent “NASA missing day” story. Matthew Henry draws extensive practical applications (the believer’s partnership with God, the honor of prayer, the church’s spiritual warfare) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-10.html; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/10.htm).

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik):** Highlights bold, public, faith-filled prayer. Joshua’s confidence to ask for the sun to stand still “before all Israel” models a faith that risks public humiliation because it rests on God’s promise. Emphasis on partnership: God did His part (hailstones, confusion), Joshua did his (all-night march, pursuing the enemy) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/).

- **Methodist/Wesleyan/Holiness:** No distinct tradition-specific reading was located from the approved sites (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu) for this passage within the search limits. The traditional reading aligns with the general Protestant literal view.

- **Lutheran (LCMS, 1517.org):** No distinct Lutheran commentary was located in the search results for this passage.

- **Catholic (Haydock’s Commentary):** Affirms the literal miracle strongly, citing Sirach 46:4 (“one day became as two”), and refutes those (Maimonides, Spinoza, Grotius) who explain it away by parhelion or reflected light. Haydock notes that God, who made all out of nothing, could easily stop the machinery of the world without deranging it. The Catholic reading also highlights the Eucharistic parallel: if God gave Joshua power over the sun, “we remark something still stronger in the power He has given to priests to consecrate the body and blood of Jesus Christ” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/joshua-10.html).

- **Orthodox (OCA.org):** No results were returned within the search limit for OCA.org on this passage.
